content.text: In the previous lesson, we explored distance-time graphs and how they represent the motion of objects. While distance-time graphs are excellent for showing an object's position over time and for calculating speed, they have limitations — they cannot directly show acceleration or tell us the direction of motion.

overcome these limitations. They are one of the most informative and widely used graphical tools in kinematics. From a single velocity-time graph, you can determine the velocity at any moment, the acceleration, and the total distance travelled. In this lesson, we will learn how to plot, interpret, and extract information from velocity-time graphs.

Since velocity is a vector, the y-axis can show both positive and negative values. Positive values typically indicate motion in one direction (e.g., forward), and negative values indicate motion in the opposite direction (e.g., backward).

Area Under the Graph Equals Distance (or Displacement)

This is because distance = speed × time, and on the graph, speed is the height and time is the width, so the area represents the product of speed and time.

For regions where velocity is positive, the area is above the time axis and represents displacement in the positive direction. For regions where velocity is negative, the area is below the time axis and represents displacement in the negative direction.

An important relationship: if you have a velocity-time graph showing constant acceleration, the corresponding distance-time graph would be a parabolic curve. If the velocity-time graph is horizontal (constant velocity), the distance-time graph is a straight line.

"You can read distance directly from the y-axis."
The y-axis shows velocity, not distance. Distance is found from the
"The area below the time axis is negative distance."

Physically, distance is always positive. The area below the axis represents displacement in the negative direction. If you want total distance, add the magnitudes of all areas. If you want net displacement, subtract the negative areas.
"Distance-time and velocity-time graphs look the same for the same journey."
They look very different. For example, an object moving at constant velocity has a horizontal velocity-time graph but a sloped distance-time graph.

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. An object can have a large velocity but zero acceleration (constant velocity), or zero velocity but large acceleration (momentarily at rest but changing velocity, like a ball at the top of its flight).
